History and Physical (Detailed)

Consult Summary:
45-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus on methotrexate presents with 1-day history of pleuritic right-sided chest/back pain, shortness of breath, low-grade subjective fever, and two episodes of hemoptysis; clinically stable on video assessment but requires same-day face-to-face review to evaluate for pneumonia or other chest pathology.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Sudden onset (today) pleuritic pain in right posterior chest when taking deep breaths, associated breathlessness.  
• Associated symptoms today: Two episodes of coughing up small amounts of blood; subjective fever (no objective temperature taken).  
• Additional history: Palpitations (“can feel my heart beating”) and progressive fatigue with reduced exercise tolerance and reduced ability to perform daily activities over the past 2 weeks.  
• No long-haul travel, no leg swelling, no known prior clots.  
• Denies smoking.  
• Review of systems otherwise not elicited.

Past Medical History:
• Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) – on methotrexate; no other complications mentioned.  
• No prior thromboembolic disease.

Medications:
• Methotrexate – dose/route/frequency not documented (taken this morning).

Allergies:
• No known drug or other allergies reported.

Social History:
• Occupation: Office desk job.  
• Residence: Lives alone in a flat; owns a cat.  
• Tobacco: Never smoker.  
• Alcohol / recreational drugs: Not discussed.

Family History:
• No family history of deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism; other family history not discussed.

Physical Examination:
(Virtual examination only)  
• Pulse: Patient-counted 11–12 beats in 10 seconds ≈ 66-72 bpm, regular.  
• Capillary refill: Normal (<2 seconds).  
• Oropharynx: Visualized, no abnormalities reported.  
• Cervical lymph nodes: Self-palpated, no enlargement.  
• No other vitals or systemic findings available.

Investigations:
• None performed during call.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Acute pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, and dyspnea; probable lower respiratory tract infection / pneumonia.  
  • Arrange same-day face-to-face GP review for full physical examination (auscultation of chest, blood pressure, temperature, repeat pulse, oxygen saturation if available).  
  • Consider chest X-ray and baseline bloods depending on examination findings.  
  • Likely start empirical oral antibiotic if bacterial infection confirmed; choice pending in-person assessment and allergy check.  
  • Provide safety-net advice: attend emergency services if worsening breathlessness, increasing hemoptysis, high fever, or chest pain.

Issue 2 – Rule-out alternative serious causes (pulmonary embolism, lung malignancy).  
  • Risk factors currently low (no flights, no clot history, non-smoker), but maintain vigilance.  
  • If symptoms persist or imaging abnormal, arrange further investigations (e.g., D-dimer, CT pulmonary angiography, or lung cancer work-up).  
  • Follow-up plan to be determined after initial clinic visit.

Issue 3 – SLE on immunosuppressive therapy.  
  • Highlight increased infection risk on methotrexate.  
  • Ensure methotrexate dosing and monitoring up to date; check recent blood counts at follow-up.  
  • Advise temporary pause of methotrexate only if instructed after in-person review.

General Plan Items:  
  • Support team phone number provided to patient to book urgent clinic slot today.  
  • Educate on red-flag symptoms and reassure low likelihood of lung cancer based on acute presentation.

Quality checks:

• Missing but expected: Objective temperature, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, full medication list with doses, complete review of systems, vaccination history.  
• Internal conflicts: Patient initially identifies as “Tracy Chapman”; clinician later addresses her as “Doris” — conflict noted.  
• Transcript quality: Generally clear; minor conversational overlaps but clinically adequate.
